title: Kunti's message before the war
hookLine: before the war, Kunti sends her sons the story of Vidula, a mother who won't let her son lie down: svadharma, your own duty, faced
carry: your own dharma is faced, not avoided
last: REPAYING KINDNESS IS DHARMA, NOT A FAVOR.

cards: Krishna's peace mission has failed. Before he leaves Hastinapura, he goes to see his aunt, who has stayed behind in the city while her sons waited out their exile. He asks if she has a message for them.
She does, but she doesn't start with advice. She starts with a story, an old one, she says, about a woman named Vidula and her son. Kunti wants her sons to hear it before the war.
Today, at the end of a week of the epics' women, Kunti speaks through someone else's voice.

teach.b: The story is in the Mahabharata's Book of Effort, here in paraphrase. Vidula is a proud woman of a warrior family. Her son Sanjaya has been beaten by a rival king, and now he lies at home, low and listless.
Vidula goes to him, and she is not gentle. Get up, she tells him. You were not born to lie here.

Then this line, which in Sanskrit runs muhurtam jvalitam shreyo, na tu dhumayitam ciram: better to blaze up for a moment than to smolder for a long time. Her son argues back: what good is a kingdom to you if I'm dead?
She answers him again and again until he rises. Then Kunti adds her own words for Arjuna and Bhima: the time has come for which a mother of warriors bears sons. Here's the teaching.
Hindus call it svadharma, your own duty, the one that's yours by your stage of life and where you stand.

Soon after, on the battlefield, Krishna tells Arjuna nearly the same thing in the Bhagavad Gita: don't give in to weakness; stand up. And: better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than another's done well.
Some readers hear courage; others hear the cost of a war a mother has just urged. The epic keeps both. And it closes a week of women: Sita, Draupadi, and Kunti, who sends a story ahead of her sons.

how: Hindus meet Kunti's message and the story of Vidula in fuller retellings and commentaries on the Mahabharata's Udyoga Parva, where it is read as a lesson about courage and duty.

o: the mother who sends her sons a story, not a command
a queen who rides into battle beside her own sons
a mother who begs her sons to make peace and stay home

s: in the Gita, Krishna says better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than another's done well
it's Gita 3.35, the same push Kunti sent through Vidula.
Vidula comforts her son and tells him to rest
she tells him to get up: better to blaze for a moment than smolder.
readers all hear Kunti's message the same way
some hear courage; others hear the cost of a war she urged.

games.q: a friend says Hindus think everyone has the exact same duty. by Kunti's message and the Gita, what fits?
o: no. svadharma is your own duty, by your stage of life and where you stand.
yes. there's one duty, the same for all.
duty stops mattering once you feel unsure.
games.why: Vidula told her son he wasn't born to lie there; Kunti sent that to Arjuna and Bhima. in the Gita, Krishna says better your own dharma, done imperfectly, than another's done well.

practice: Ask gently what is yours to do right now, as a student, a parent, a friend, a worker, and whether one part of it has been smoldering a long time. Don't scold yourself: Vidula's words were for a warrior, and yours can be kinder.
Let it come into view, warmth gathering around it like an ember on each breath in, one first step appearing on each breath out. If you pray, you can ask for courage.
And if low days ever start to feel like there's no point, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Kunti. Before the war, she sent her sons Vidula's story: blaze a moment, don't smolder. Today's word.

orig.s: मुहूर्तं ज्वलितं श्रेयो न तु धूमायितं चिरम्
orig.say: moo-HOOR-tum JVUH-li-tum SHRAY-yoh nuh too dhoo-MAH-yi-tum CHI-rum
orig.note: Sanskrit, from Vidula's words to her son: better to blaze up for a moment than to smolder for a long time.

carryVoice: Your line: your own dharma is faced, not avoided. Kunti sent her sons Vidula's story. That's a week of the epics' women.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva, Kunti's message to the Pandavas through Krishna; the Vidula passage (Vidulaputranushasana) (Critical Edition 5.130–134; Ganguli sections 132–136)
Bhagavata Purana 1.8.25 (Kunti asks for troubles; recalled from day 1335)
